content.text: Extract Hyperlinks scans a PDF for all embedded URLs and outputs them as a deduplicated JSON list. The tool searches two sources: Link annotations (clickable links in the PDF) and text content (URLs that appear as plain text on the page).

Using pdf.js, the tool iterates over every page, extracts Link annotations with their URL properties, and also performs regex matching on the text content for http:// and https:// URLs. Both sources are merged and deduplicated to produce the final list.

The output is a JSON file containing a single array of unique URLs, one per line. This is useful for link auditing, verifying hyperlink integrity, and cataloging references in research documents or legal filings.

The regex matching covers both http:// and https:// protocols, as well as URLs starting with www. that may not have an explicit protocol prefix. URLs with special characters like query parameters, fragments, and encoded characters are captured as long as they appear on a single text line.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.subHeading: Does it extract URLs from Link annotations AND text content?

content.text: Yes. Both sources are searched. Link annotations are clickable links embedded in the PDF. Text-based URLs are plain-text URLs that appear on the page but aren't clickable. Both are merged into a single deduplicated list.

sections.subHeading: Are the URLs deduplicated?

content.text: Yes. If the same URL appears as both a Link annotation and as text, or appears on multiple pages, it appears only once in the output. The deduplication uses exact string matching.

sections.subHeading: What if the PDF has no hyperlinks?

content.text: The tool returns an empty array: { links: [] }. This is common for scanned documents or text-only PDFs that contain no interactive elements or URL text.

sections.subHeading: Does it extract mailto: links from annotations?

content.text: Not currently. Only http/https URLs from Link annotations and text content are extracted. Mailto: links in annotations are a different annotation subtype and are not included in this extraction.

Extract Headings identifies heading-like text in a PDF by detecting lines with larger-than-normal font sizes. The tool uses pdf.js to extract text content, calculates the font size of each text item, and flags lines where the maximum font size exceeds 14pt.

For each detected heading, the output includes the page number, the heading text, and the font size. The detection heuristic looks for text lines that are shorter than 60 characters and longer than 3 characters — filtering out body text that happens to use a large font.

The output is a JSON array of heading objects, sorted by page number. This is useful for understanding document structure, generating tables of contents, or verifying that heading hierarchy is consistent across the document.

The font size calculation uses the Euclidean norm of the text matrix transformation vectors, which correctly handles rotated and scaled text. This means headings that are rotated 90 degrees or scaled non-uniformly are still detected by their effective font size.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.subHeading: What font size threshold determines a heading?

content.text: Lines with a maximum font size above 14pt are flagged as potential headings. This threshold works for most standard documents where body text is 10-12pt and headings are 14pt or larger. Documents with unusual font sizes may need manual adjustment of the threshold.

sections.subHeading: Does it detect heading levels (H1, H2, H3)?

content.text: Not explicitly. The tool reports the font size for each heading, which can be used to infer relative levels (larger font = higher-level heading). It does not map to specific HTML heading levels.

sections.subHeading: What about multi-line headings?

content.text: The tool detects headings line by line. If a heading spans multiple lines, each line is reported separately. The output can be post-processed to group consecutive lines on the same page as a single heading.

sections.subHeading: Why the 14pt threshold?

content.text: 14pt is a common minimum for heading text in standard documents where body text is typically 10-12pt. Documents with larger body text may produce false positives. The threshold is hardcoded and cannot be adjusted per-document.

Extract Email Addresses scans all text content in a PDF and identifies email addresses using a regex pattern. The tool uses pdf.js to extract text from every page, then matches against the standard email pattern (user@domain.tld).
The output is a JSON file containing a deduplicated array of all email addresses found in the document. Both annotated email links and plain-text email addresses visible on the page are captured.

This is a read-only extraction tool — it does not modify the PDF or send any data externally. The email list is useful for contact harvesting from documents, compliance audits, and data processing workflows.

The regex pattern matches standard email formats with at least one character before the @ symbol, a domain with at least one dot, and a top-level domain of at least 2 characters. This filters out most false positives while catching legitimate addresses in the document text.

sections.subHeading: Does it extract emails from annotations or only text?

content.text: Text content only. Mailto: link annotations are not currently extracted — only email addresses that appear as visible text on the page are matched.

sections.subHeading: How accurate is the email detection?

content.text: The regex pattern matches standard email formats (user@domain.tld). It may produce false positives for text that looks like an email but isn't (like code snippets or configuration strings). It may miss emails split across text items by pdf.js rendering.

sections.subHeading: Does it handle internationalized email addresses?

content.text: The pattern matches ASCII email addresses. Internationalized email addresses with non-ASCII characters in the domain or local part may not be detected by the current regex.

sections.subHeading: What about email addresses split across text items?

content.text: pdf.js may split a single email address across multiple text items if the PDF was created with individual character positioning. In that case, the email may not be detected because the @ symbol and domain are in separate text items. This is a known limitation of text-based extraction from PDFs.

Extract Phone Numbers scans all text content in a PDF and identifies phone numbers using a regex pattern that matches common international and domestic formats. The tool uses pdf.js to extract text from every page, then matches against patterns like (555) 123-4567, +1-555-123-4567, and 555.123.4567.

The output is a JSON file containing a deduplicated array of all phone numbers found in the document. The tool handles various separators (dashes, dots, spaces, parentheses) and optional country codes.
This is a read-only extraction tool. The phone number list is useful for contact harvesting, PII audits, and building contact databases from documents.

The regex pattern handles US phone number formats with various separators including parentheses, dashes, dots, and spaces. The optional country code prefix is captured when present. The pattern requires exactly 10 digits for the main number after stripping formatting characters.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.subHeading: What phone number formats are detected?

content.text: The pattern matches US-style numbers with optional country code: (555) 123-4567, 555-123-4567, 555.123.4567, +1-555-123-4567, and variations. International formats with different digit groupings may not be fully matched.

sections.subHeading: Can it detect fax numbers separately from phone numbers?

content.text: No. The tool extracts all numbers matching the phone pattern regardless of context. If the document labels some numbers as fax, you would need to review the output manually or use text search to filter.

sections.subHeading: What about extension numbers?

content.text: The pattern does not capture extensions (like x1234 or ext. 123). Only the main phone number is extracted. Extensions that appear as separate text items after the number are not included.

sections.subHeading: Does it handle international formats like +44 20 7946 0958?

content.text: The pattern primarily matches US-style formats. International numbers with different digit groupings like UK 11-digit numbers or German area codes may not be fully matched. The pattern is designed for common North American formats.

sections.subHeading: What about toll-free numbers like 1-800-FLOWERS?

content.text: The pattern matches numeric formats only. Vanity numbers with letters (1-800-FLOWERS) are not matched because the letters are not converted to digits. Only purely numeric phone number patterns are detected.

Extract Tables identifies tabular data in a PDF and exports each detected table as a separate CSV file. The tool uses pdf.js to extract text items, groups them by vertical position (Y coordinate) to identify rows, and detects tables by counting rows with 3 or more items.

Rows with 3 or more text items on the same horizontal line are treated as table rows. Consecutive table rows are grouped into a single table. When no tables are detected, the tool falls back to exporting all text as a single CSV.
The output is a zip archive containing one CSV file per detected table (table-1.csv, table-2.csv, etc.). Each CSV contains the table rows with cells quoted and comma-separated.

The row grouping uses a 5-point Y-coordinate tolerance to handle slight vertical misalignment between text items on the same logical row. Text items within 5 points of the same Y position are grouped together, then sorted left-to-right by their X coordinate to preserve column order.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.subHeading: How does the tool detect table boundaries?

content.text: Text items on the same horizontal line (within 5 points of the same Y coordinate) are grouped into a row. Rows with 3 or more items are flagged as table rows. Consecutive table rows are grouped into a single table. A non-table row (fewer than 3 items) breaks the table boundary.

sections.subHeading: What about merged cells or complex table layouts?

content.text: The tool does not detect merged cells. Each text item becomes its own cell. Merged cells may appear as a single cell spanning what should be multiple columns, or as separate cells with repeated content.

sections.subHeading: What happens if no tables are found?

content.text: The tool falls back to exporting all text content as a single CSV file (fallback-text.csv), with each row containing all text items from that line. This ensures you always get output, even if the table detection heuristic doesn't match the document layout.

sections.subHeading: How does it handle tables with borders or lines?

content.text: The tool does not detect table borders or lines - it only uses text item positions. Tables defined by visual borders but containing sparse text may not be detected as tables. The tool works best with text-heavy tables where items are clearly aligned in rows and columns.
PDF Size Analyzer reports the file size of a PDF document in both bytes and megabytes. The tool reads the file metadata to provide a quick size assessment without processing the document content.

The output is a JSON file containing the filename, total bytes, and total megabytes. This basic metadata is useful for quick file assessment before processing, upload size verification, and storage planning.
For more detailed analysis including page count, image sizes, and font information, use the PDF Statistics tool which provides comprehensive document metrics.

While this tool only reports file size, understanding what drives PDF size is useful context. The largest contributors to PDF file size are typically embedded images especially uncompressed or high-resolution ones, embedded fonts where full font subsets can add hundreds of KB per font, XMP metadata streams, and embedded attachments. A 10-page text-only PDF is usually under 100KB, while the same document with high-resolution images can easily exceed 10MB.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.subHeading: Does this analyze the content or just report file size?

content.text: Just file size. For content analysis (page count, image sizes, font usage), use the PDF Statistics tool instead. This tool is designed for quick size assessment without processing the document.

sections.subHeading: What if the file is very large?

content.text: File size is read from metadata, so even very large files (hundreds of MB) are processed instantly. The tool does not read the file content, only its size.

sections.subHeading: Why would a simple text PDF be large?

content.text: Text PDFs can be large if they embed full font subsets including glyphs not used in the document, contain high-resolution scanned page images behind the text, or include embedded attachments and metadata streams. The file size reflects the total of all embedded resources, not just the visible text.

sections.subHeading: How does compressed vs uncompressed PDF affect size?

content.text: PDFs using FlateDecode compression (the standard) are typically 5-10x smaller than uncompressed equivalents. PDFs with embedded JPEG images compress well, while those with uncompressed bitmaps or full font subsets remain large regardless of text content.

Version Checker reads the PDF header to determine the PDF specification version used to create the document. The tool reads the first 50 bytes of the file, looks for the %PDF-X.Y signature, and reports the version number.

The output is a JSON file containing the filename and PDF version (like 1.4, 1.5, 1.7, or 2.0). The version indicates which PDF specification features the document may use, which is important for compatibility with PDF readers and processing tools.
This is a lightweight inspection that reads only the file header — it does not parse the full document structure. The check completes instantly regardless of file size.

Different PDF versions enable different features: PDF 1.4 (Acrobat 5) introduced transparency and layers; PDF 1.5 (Acrobat 6) added JPEG2000 compression, object streams, and XMP metadata; PDF 1.6 (Acrobat 7) added extended security and 3D annotations; PDF 1.7 (Acrobat 8) added improved compression and annotation support; PDF 2.0 (ISO 32000-2) added rich media, 3D, and improved encryption. Knowing the version helps predict which features a document may use.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.subHeading: What PDF versions are detected?

content.text: Any version specified in the PDF header: 1.0 through 2.0. The most common versions are 1.4 (Acrobat 5), 1.5 (Acrobat 6), 1.6 (Acrobat 7), 1.7 (Acrobat 8), and 2.0 (ISO 32000-2).

sections.subHeading: What if the version shows as Unknown?

content.text: The file may not be a valid PDF, or the header may be corrupted. Non-PDF files uploaded by mistake will show Unknown since they lack the %PDF-X.Y signature.

sections.subHeading: Does the version affect how the PDF renders?

content.text: Yes. Higher versions support more features (transparency, layers, JPEG2000 compression, XMP metadata). A PDF created with version 1.7 features may not render correctly in readers that only support version 1.4.

sections.subHeading: Can a PDF claim a version but use features from a different version?

content.text: Yes. Some PDF producers set the version header higher than necessary, or embed features from newer versions in an older-version document. The header version indicates what the creator declared, not necessarily what features are actually used.

sections.subHeading: Does PDF/A compliance require a specific version?

content.text: Yes. PDF/A-1 requires PDF 1.4, PDF/A-2 allows PDF 1.5-1.7, and PDF/A-3 allows PDF 1.5-1.7. PDF/A-4 is based on PDF 2.0. The version check helps determine which PDF/A level a document might conform to.

sections.subHeading: Can attachments contain malware?

sections.subHeading: Can attachments be hidden or obfuscated?

sections.subHeading: What is the maximum attachment size?

content.text: There is no PDF specification limit on attachment size, but some PDF readers may struggle with very large attachments (over 100MB). The inspector reports the size so you can assess whether extraction will be practical.

sections.subHeading: What metrics are included in the statistics?

sections.subHeading: How long does the analysis take?

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.subHeading: What metadata fields are extracted?

content.text: Title, author, subject, keywords, creator (application that created the PDF), producer (application that produced it), creation date, modification date, and any custom metadata entries in the document information dictionary.

sections.subHeading: Can metadata be faked or misleading?

content.text: Yes. PDF metadata is user-editable and can be modified by any PDF editor. Creation dates, author names, and other fields should not be relied upon as proof of authenticity without additional verification. For authenticated timestamps, use the Timestamp PDF tool.

sections.subHeading: Does it extract XMP metadata?

content.text: The tool extracts the standard document information dictionary. XMP metadata (stored in a separate metadata stream) may not be fully captured by this tool. For comprehensive XMP extraction, a specialized XMP parser would be needed.

sections.subHeading: What date format is used?

content.text: PDF metadata dates follow the D:YYYYMMDDHHmmSS format (for example D:20240115143000 for January 15, 2024 at 2:30 PM). Timezone offsets may be appended. The tool preserves the original format in the JSON output.
Page Dimensions reports the width and height of every page in a PDF, measured in points (1 point = 1/72 inch). The tool uses pdf-lib to read each page's MediaBox and report its dimensions.

PDF dimensions are measured in points where 1 point equals 1/72 inch. Common sizes include A4 at 595.28 x 841.89 points (210 x 297mm), US Letter at 612 x 792 points (8.5 x 11 inches), and US Legal at 612 x 1008 points (8.5 x 14 inches). The tool reads the MediaBox array from each page dictionary, which defines the physical page boundaries.

Click Check Dimensions. The tool reads the MediaBox of every page.
A download button appears with page-dimensions.json listing each page's width, height, and detected size.

content.text: Print shops need exact page dimensions to configure their RIP (Raster Image Processor) settings. Incorrect dimensions cause scaling errors, cropped content, or wasted paper.
Document preparers merging PDFs from different sources need to verify that page sizes are consistent. Mixed dimensions in a merged document can cause layout issues in viewers and printers.
PDF/A compliance requires specific page dimension ranges. Checking dimensions before submission ensures the document meets archival format requirements.

Print production teams need exact dimensions to configure imposition software, cutting templates, and binding equipment. Even small dimension mismatches can cause content to be trimmed or misaligned in the final printed product.

Your files never leave your browser. Every step — reading page MediaBox values and generating the JSON output — happens on your own device using pdf-lib. Nothing is uploaded to Racira's servers, no copies are stored in the cloud, and no file data is transmitted at any point.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.subHeading: What standard sizes are detected?

content.text: A4 (595.28 x 841.89 pt), US Letter (612 x 792 pt), US Legal (612 x 1008 pt), A3 (841.89 x 1190.55 pt), and A5 (419.53 x 595.28 pt). Pages that don't match standard sizes are reported as Custom.

sections.subHeading: Does it report CropBox or just MediaBox?

content.text: The tool reports MediaBox dimensions, which represent the physical page size. CropBox, TrimBox, and BleedBox (which define visible and print areas) are not separately reported.

sections.subHeading: What if pages have different sizes?

content.text: Each page is reported individually. If a document has mixed page sizes, the output will show different dimensions for different pages, making it easy to identify which pages need resizing.

sections.subHeading: What about pages with different orientations?

content.text: Each page is reported independently. A document with mixed portrait and landscape pages will show different dimensions for different pages. The tool does not detect or report orientation - only raw width and height values.

sections.subHeading: What is the difference between MediaBox and CropBox?

content.text: MediaBox defines the physical page size. CropBox defines the visible area (what the user sees). If CropBox is set and smaller than MediaBox, only the CropBox area is displayed. This tool reports MediaBox, which is the actual page size.

Certificate Inspector extracts and displays detailed information about digital certificates embedded in a PDF document. The tool uses node-forge to parse X.509 certificates from the PDF's signature dictionaries and reports the certificate chain, issuer, subject, validity dates, and key information.

The output is a JSON file containing certificate details for each digital signature found in the document. This includes the certificate hierarchy, trust chain status, expiration information, and the signing algorithm used.

This tool complements the Validate Signature tool by providing the raw certificate data rather than just a validity verdict. It is useful for detailed certificate chain analysis and trust verification.

The certificate chain typically has 2-3 levels: the end-entity certificate used to sign the document, one or more intermediate CA certificates, and the root CA certificate. The inspector reports each level separately, showing the issuer-subject relationship that forms the trust chain. Self-signed certificates where issuer equals subject appear at the root level.

items: Drop a signed PDF onto the upload zone, or click to browse and select it.
Click Inspect Certificates. The tool parses the signature dictionaries and extracts X.509 certificate data.
A download button appears with certificates.json containing the certificate chain details for each signature.

content.text: Security teams verifying document signatures need to examine the certificate chain to determine whether the signing certificate was issued by a trusted CA. The inspector provides the raw data needed for this analysis.

Compliance auditors verifying digital signature validity check certificate expiration dates, key sizes, and signing algorithms against organizational policies. The inspector provides all this data in a structured format.
PKI administrators debugging signature verification failures use the certificate inspector to identify which certificate in the chain is causing the issue — expired, revoked, or untrusted.

PKI administrators validating signing certificates against their organization trust store need the full certificate chain data to verify that each link in the chain is valid and trusted. The inspector provides the raw data needed for this verification.

Your files never leave your browser. Every step — parsing PDF signature dictionaries, extracting X.509 certificates, and generating the JSON output — happens on your own device using node-forge. Nothing is uploaded to Racira's servers, no copies are stored in the cloud, and no file data is transmitted at any point.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.subHeading: What certificate information is extracted?

content.text: Subject distinguished name, issuer distinguished name, serial number, validity period (not-before and not-after dates), public key algorithm and size, signature algorithm, and certificate chain hierarchy.

sections.subHeading: Does it verify the certificate against a CA store?

content.text: The tool extracts and displays the certificate data but does not perform online OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) or CRL (Certificate Revocation List) checks. Trust verification against a CA store would require a separate PKI verification step.

sections.subHeading: What if the PDF has no digital signatures?

content.text: The tool reports that no digital signatures were found. Note that visual signatures (stamped images) do not contain certificates — only cryptographic digital signatures have embedded X.509 certificates.

sections.subHeading: What if the certificate chain is incomplete?

content.text: The tool reports whatever certificates are present in the signature. If intermediate certificates are missing, which is a common issue, the chain will appear truncated. Incomplete chains may cause validation failures in strict PDF readers.
